evidence: Cic. Off. 3.37 (Lewis & Short): sī modo in philosophiā aliquid prōfēcimus
Quint. 10.1.112: ille sē prōfēcisse sciat, cui Cicerō valdē placēbit
terms.comment: Of progress in learning or a skill, often with aliquid, multum or nihil: nihil prōficere is to get nowhere. Traupman’s word for improving in one’s studies; his noun for “improvement” is prōfectus.

evidence: Hor. Epist. 2.2.211: lēnior et melior fīs accēdente senectā?
terms.comment: Of a person or a thing becoming better in any way.

evidence: Sen. Ep. 47.21: saepe mūtātur, nōn in melius, sed in aliud

terms.gloss: be a little better (after an illness)
terms.register: vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut.; Cic. in epistulīs
evidence: Cic. Fam. 16.5.1: cum meliusculē tibi esset
terms.comment: With a dative of the person. A rare adverb: Lewis & Short cites this line of Cicero’s, Fronto, and Plautus in another sense. To recover from an illness is convalēscere (see I feel better).
Lewis & Short: poetic and post-Augustan prose.

phrases.latin: nātālīs grātē numerās? ignōscis amīcīs? lēnior et melior fīs accēdente senectā?
phrases.english: Do you count your birthdays gratefully? Do you forgive your friends? Are you growing gentler and better as old age comes on?

phrases.latin: ille sē prōfēcisse sciat, cui Cicerō valdē placēbit
phrases.english: Let a man know that he has made progress when Cicero delights him.
“How far will I get?” you ask. As far as you try.
to feel somewhat better (of a patient)
We are making some headway, I hope.
